33. Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding the truth of facts therein stated.-
Evidence given by a witness in a judicial proceeding, or before any person authorized by law to take it, is relevant for the purpose of proving, in a subsequent judicial proceeding, or in a later stage of the same judicial proceeding, the truth of the facts which it states, when the witness is dead or cannot be found, or is incapable of giving evidence, or is kept out of the way by the adverse party, or if his presence cannot be obtained without an amount of - 23 - delay or expense which, under the circumstances of the case, the Court considers unreasonable:
Provided- that the proceeding was between the same parties or their representatives in interest;
that the adverse party in the first proceeding had the right and opportunity to cross-examine;

sentences.text: Explanation.-
A criminal trial or inquiry shall be deemed to be a proceeding between the prosecutor and the accused within the meaning of this section.
30. Thus, Section 33 of Evidence Act deals with the relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceedings, the truth of facts therein stated.

This section provides that the evidence given by the witness in earlier judicial proceedings or before any person authorised by law to take evidence is relevant in a subsequent judicial proceedings or a later stage of same judicial proceedings, for the purpose of proving truth of facts contained therein, if certain conditions mentioned in the section are satisfied.
The death of a witness whose evidence is admitted should first be proved unless it is admitted on the other side.

The Hon'ble Apex court in V M Mathew V/S S Sharma (1995) 6 SCC 122, (AIR 1996 SC 109), held that, in view of the provision of Sec 33 of Evidence Act, evidence of a witness in a previous proceedings would be admissible under section 33 of the Act only if the adverse party in the 1st proceeding had the right and opportunity to cross examine the witness.

sentences.text:
32. The words "that the adverse party in the 1st proceeding had the right and opportunity to cross examine'' used in second proviso of sec 33 of the evidence act cannot be stretched to be interpreted to mean 'that the adverse party had actually cross examined such witness'.
33.

More so, the 2nd proviso of Sec 33 of evidence Act deals with witness cross examined in a previous proceeding' but in the present case at hand, the opportunity to cross examine was very much available to the accused in the same proceedings and not referrable to any subsequent proceeding or at a later stage in same - 25 - proceeding, which may be a case.
Hence, the arguments advanced by the counsel for the petitioner based on 2nd proviso to sec 33 of evidence act cannot be acceptable.
34. The evidence untested by cross examination has no evidenciary value but such evidence cannot be rejected as inadmiisible.
The correct rule is that the evidence is admissible but the weight to be attached to such evidence should depend on the circumstances of each case.
We have to consider the probative value of the evidence recorded of the witnesses of which the court may act upon.
The court should look at the evidence carefully to see that such a testimony of a witness was likely to be seriously shaken or his good faith to be successfully impeached.

It is settled principles of law that, if the evidence is inadmissible the court is not entitled to consider it at all, whereas if it is admissible the courts must decide on the circumstances of each case, whether any weight to be attached or not.
